newsitem.title: USA: Recent remarks show Fed wary of strong U.S. growth.
newsitem.headline: Recent remarks show Fed wary of strong U.S. growth.

text.p: A review of recent speeches by several Federal Reserve Bank presidents show they remain wary about underlying strength in the economy as they go into this year's third meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on May 20.
Recent remarks also show how unanimous top Fed officials are in their commitment to preemptive monetary policy. Many suggested they expect some uptick in inflation in 1997.

The Fed's policy-setting body meets on Tuesday to deliberate on monetary policy. The central bank last changed interest rates on March 25, when it raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.
The announcement of the outcome of the meeting is expected at around 1415 EDT/1815 GMT.
The following comments are divided by topics and were all made by regional Federal Reserve Bank presidents after the March 25 FOMC meeting.
*** ECONOMIC GROWTH ***
SAN FRANCISCO FED'S ROBERT PARRY:

Parry said recently he expected "a fairly significant" slowdown in the economy in the second quarter of the year following a red hot rate of 5.6 percent Gross Domestic Product growth seen in the first three months of the year.
He stressed the need for slower growth to avoid future inflation problems.
PHILADELPHIA FED'S EDWARD BOEHNE:

Boehne recently said the Fed's preemptive monetary policy prolongued the economic expansion in 1994, and chances were that the central bank can do the same in 1997. "In 1994, when interest rates were raised to avoid overheating, we were succesful in prolonging the expansion and job creation through preemptive action.
"I think we have a good chance to do the same in 1997," he said.
RICHMOND FED'S ALFRED BROADDUS:
Citing a consensus of professional forecasters, Broaddus recently said GDP was expected to slow slightly to below 3.0 percent by the end of 1997
KANSAS CITY FED'S THOMAS HOENIG:
Hoenig said he believes the economy is still growing at a healthy clip. "Virtually all sectors of the economy are growing solidly," he said.
MINNEAPOLIS FED'S GARY STERN:
Stern said the economy was set for another year of balanced growth.
*** INFLATION ***
SAN FRANCISCO FED'S ROBERT PARRY:
Parry said the current level of economic resource utilization was not sustainable in the long run without triggering inflationary pressures.
"The current level of resource utilization is not sustainable without inflation becoming a problem," he said.
PHILADELPHIA FED'S EDWARD BOEHNE:

In his latest speech, Boehne said the Fed's ultimate monetary policy goal was to promote "maximum sustainable growth." He stressed the need for the Fed to be preemptive, though, saying that it is important to contain inflationary pressures "before they take root."
RICHMOND FED'S ALFRED BROADDUS:

The Fed official said he did not expect inflation to boom in 1997 despite very tight labor markets. He said, however, he expected inflation to show an uptick in 1997, with the core Consumer Price Index projected to remain below 3.0 percent.
KANSAS CITY FED'S THOMAS HOENIG:
The official said in his latest public speech that the evidence remained mixed, but signs suggested inflationary risks were "on the upside."
"To be sure, the evidence is mixed, but there are signs that inflation risks are on the upside," he said.
MINNEAPOLIS FED'S GARY STERN:
Stern said the Fed's preemptive approach to fighting inflation justified the Fed's 25 basis-point rate hike on the federal funds rate to 5.50 percent on March 25.
He stressed the need for the Fed's monetary policy to remain preemptive.
*** LABOR MARKETS ***
SAN FRANCISCO FED'S ROBERT PARRY:

Parry said he saw the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU) at around 5.5 percent. In a recent interview, he said a jobless rate below that level might create inflationary pressures.
"I suggest that something around 5.5 percent would be the number one should look at, and if it were to be less than that for a prolonged period of time, you have to become a bit concerned," he said.
RICHMOND FED'S ALFRED BROADDUS:

Broaddus recently said labor markets were tight and were expected to remain tight throughout 1997. He said he expected the unemployment rate to be around 5.0 percent by the end of the year, virtually unchanged from the 4.9 percent level measured by the Labor Department in April.
Broaddus said the current economic scenario suggests the risks remain tilted to the upside for the U.S. economy.
KANSAS CITY FED'S THOMAS HOENIG:

Hoening said labor markets were tightening, which could lead to future upward price pressures. "Anecdotal reports here in the 10th (Fed) district and elsewhere suggest labor markets are tightening," he said.
MINNEAPOLIS FED'S GARY STERN:

Stern said recently there was no question that many labor markets were tight. He also said scattered labor shortages and mild wage inflation also helped to explain the Fed's need to tighten credit at the March 25 meeting.
Another factor seen as key for Tuesday's FOMC meting was the level of consumer spending.

Demand was extremely strong in the first quarter of the year, but some regional Fed economists and ex-central bank officials have detected signs, albeit incipient, of a cooling off in demand in the second quarter.
Philadelphia Fed's vice-president Ted Crone said regional consumers were "a little more cautious" now than they were a few months ago.
Ex-Fed Vice Chairman Alan Blinder said consumer spending appeared to be simmering down after two months of weak retail sales data.
